concept.title: Inherit, reset and roll back values
concept.shortdesc: An element that no rule sets a property for still gets a value. It takes the value of its parent or the initial value of the property. You can ask for either, or for a value from an earlier step of the cascade, with the keywords inherit, initial, unset, revert and revert-layer.

section.title: Inheritance
section.p: Some properties are inherited: an element takes the value that its parent has, unless a rule gives it another one. Text properties are inherited, such as color, font-family, font-size, font-weight, line-height and text-align. So you can set them once on an element high in the tree:
The title is teal. All the other descendants of the chapter are navy and 11 points large.

fig.title: An inherited and a not inherited property

image.alt: A chapter box with a color and a left margin, and two boxes below it, a title and a para. Both children show the color of the chapter, as inherited, and a left margin of 0, the initial value, because the margin is not inherited.

section.p: Properties that describe boxes are not inherited, such as margin, padding, border, background-color and display. If a rule gives the chapter a border, its titles have no border. An element without a value for such a property uses the initial value of the property.
Inheritance follows the tree of your XML. The reference tables of this guide give the initial value of each property in the column Default.

section.title: Keywords that choose where a value comes from
section.p: You can write these keywords as the whole value of any property:

ul.li: inherit takes the value of the parent, even for a property that is not inherited. On the root element, which has no parent, it gives the initial value.
initial takes the initial value of the property, even for a property that is inherited.
unset is inherit for an inherited property, and initial for the others. It is the natural state of a property that no rule sets.

revert removes your declarations for the property from this element, and lets the property have the value it would have without your stylesheet. CSSMedia has almost no rules of its own, so this is usually the same as unset.
revert-layer removes the declarations of the layer of the rule, and lets the layers below it decide.

section.p: The title has the same left margin as its parent. The note is black, even if its parent is navy.
The keyword revert-layer is useful in a layer that adds to the one below it:
The rule of the layer theme gives the title the value that the layer base gives it. In a layer with nothing below, revert-layer acts as revert.

section.title: Resetting everything with all
section.p: The property all takes one of the keywords above and applies it to every property at once, except direction, unicode-bidi and custom properties:

This note starts without any style from the rules of its ancestors, and the declarations after all build it again. Remember that all: initial also resets display, which is inline initially, so write it again for an element that must be a block.

section.title: A value that is invalid when it is computed
section.p: A declaration with a value that CSSMedia cannot read is ignored before the cascade starts, so another declaration for the property can win. A declaration whose value uses var() is different, because CSSMedia can check it only after the cascade has chosen it. If the substituted value is not valid for the property, for example because the custom property does not exist, the declaration acts as unset. CSSMedia does not go back to a declaration that lost:

The title does not become red. The second declaration won, it is not valid, and the title takes the color of its parent. Write a fallback, as var(--missing, red), to avoid this. Reuse values with custom properties and functions explains var().
